rules.statement: Prototypical nouns distinguish singular and plural number and plain and genitive case, yielding singular plain, singular genitive, plural plain, and plural genitive forms.
rules.condition: For a prototypical noun lexeme with both singular and plural forms, the paradigm crosses the number distinction (singular/plural) with the case distinction (plain/genitive).

exceptions.description: Not all nouns have both number forms: equipment has no plural counterpart, while outskirts has no singular counterpart; the chapter defers the wider treatment to §3.2.

contrast.text: dog / dog’s / dogs / dogs’ [singular plain, singular genitive, plural plain, plural genitive]
child / child’s / children / children’s [singular plain, singular genitive, plural plain, plural genitive]
equipment [no plural counterpart in the cited example]
outskirts [no singular counterpart in the cited example]

rules.statement: Certain determinatives, pre-head adjective phrases, and relative clauses occur exclusively or almost exclusively with nouns as head.
rules.condition: When a noun heads an NP or nominal, its dependent set may include noun-associated determinatives, pre-head AdjPs, and relative clauses, which occur exclusively or almost exclusively with nouns as head.

contrast.text: a lantern [determinative with noun head]
bright lanterns [pre-head AdjP with noun head]
lanterns that glow [relative clause with noun head]
every weekend [determinative with noun head]

sources.section: §1 Distinctive properties of nouns and NPs

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source material for this concept was supplied or found in the repository's expected source directory.

rules.review_notes: The source says 'exclusively or almost exclusively'; this is a distributional generalization, not an absolute restriction.

rules.statement: A noun does not take a direct object, unlike a verb; nominal dependents that express related content are not direct objects of the noun.
rules.condition: When a noun functions as the head of a nominal, it cannot be followed by an NP functioning as its direct object; a related dependent may instead occur in a construction licensed by the noun, such as a PP.
rules.violation: A noun head is analysed as taking a bare NP direct object, as though it were a transitive verb.

correct.note: The verb takes the direct object NP.

correct.text: The students’ criticism of the decision was clear.
correct.note: The noun is followed by a PP, not a direct object.
The verb takes the direct object NP.

correct.text: The guide’s description of the route was accurate.
correct.note: The noun is followed by a PP, not a direct object.

incorrect.text: *The students’ criticism the decision was clear.
*The guide’s description the route was accurate.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: noun complementation; nouns do not take objects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source material for this concept was supplied or found in the repository's expected source directory.

rules.review_notes: The contrast concerns the grammatical relation object, not the broader ability of nouns to take complements. The examples use PP dependents in the acceptable nominal constructions.

rules.concept: functions of NPs beyond clause complements
rules.statement: Besides subject, object, and predicative-complement functions in clause structure, NPs can function as PP complements, subject-determiners in NPs, clause adjuncts, modifiers in AdjPs, AdvPs and PPs, supplements, and vocatives.
rules.condition: When classifying an NP in context, consider the larger constituent it combines with: an NP may be a complement within a PP, a subject-determiner inside a larger NP, an adjunct or modifier, a supplement, or a vocative rather than a clause-level subject, object, or predicative complement.

exceptions.description: The source says the adjunct, modifier, supplement, and vocative functions illustrated in [6iii–ix] accept only a restricted range of NPs; one or two NP expressions are specialised for modifying functions and do not occur as clause complements.

contrast.text: The hikers spoke to the guide. [the guide: complement of a preposition]
Mara’s notes were missing. [Mara’s: subject-determiner in an NP]
We waited three hours. [three hours: clause adjunct]
The shelf was two metres high. [two metres: modifier in an AdjP]
They arrived two hours late. [two hours: modifier in an AdvP]
The wreck lay a mile under the sea. [a mile: modifier in a PP]
We met Lina, an experienced guide. [an experienced guide: supplement]
Ava, your taxi is here. [Ava: vocative]
contrast.note: Illustrates a non-clausal NP function; the source restricts the range of NPs available for this and related peripheral functions.

rules.review_notes: The subject-determiner function is already represented by PHR-010; this record adds the broader inventory of NP functions and does not recreate that rule. The source's restricted-distribution caveat is retained.

rules.statement: The semantically empty dummy there qualifies as an NP because it occurs in at least one of the clause-complement positions, most clearly as subject in an existential construction.
rules.condition: When determining whether a noun-headed unit belongs to the NP category, occurrence in at least one of subject, object, or predicative-complement function is sufficient; dummy there qualifies through subject function and also occurs as object in a related raised-object construction.

exceptions.description: Dummy there does not occur in all three major clause-complement positions; the source only establishes subject use and the related raised-object use.

contrast.text: There are several options available. [dummy there as subject]
I believe there to be several options available. [dummy there in a raised-object construction]

rules.statement: A determinerless bare role expression such as president or deputy leader of the party qualifies as an NP when it functions as a predicative complement.
rules.condition: When a determinerless noun phrase denotes a role and functions as the predicative complement of a verb such as be, become, appoint, or elect, classify it as an NP despite the absence of a determiner.

contrast.text: Mira hopes to become president. [president: bare role NP as predicative complement]
The members elected Noor deputy leader. [deputy leader: bare role NP as predicative complement]
